summary: A landlocked mountainous country in Central Asia, crossed by the Tian Shan range and home to Lake Issyk-Kul, known for its nomadic culture and the epic Manas; it became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam spread first in cities such as Osh in the Fergana Valley, while the nomadic Kyrgyz were gradually Islamized during Kokand Khanate rule in the 17th–19th centuries. Religion was suppressed in the Soviet period, and after independence in 1991 many mosques were built with funding from countries such as Saudi Arabia and Turkey; the south is more conservative and the north more secular, and Islamic identity has also become part of Kyrgyz national identity.

ranking.name: Russian Orthodoxy
ranking.description: After the Russian Empire annexed the Kokand Khanate in 1876, large numbers of Russian and Ukrainian peasants moved into the Chuy Valley in the north, and in the Soviet period more Slavic workers and technicians moved into the capital Bishkek. They are Orthodox; after independence in 1991 many returned to Russia, so the Orthodox share declined.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: This includes the various Protestant denominations (brought in by Western missionaries after independence), Catholicism, the Baha'i Faith, Buddhism, and people with no religious affiliation after Soviet atheist education. In addition, many Kyrgyz still retain traditional elements of belief such as ancestor spirit and holy-site worship.

religion.background: The Kyrgyz traditionally followed Tengrism (the sky-god faith) and shamanism; in the 8th century, after the Battle of Talas (751), the Arabs expanded their influence in Central Asia, and Islam spread first in the settled cities of the Fergana Valley. The nomadic Kyrgyz were generally Islamized only in the 17th–19th centuries under Kokand Khanate rule and Sufi influence, and kept many pre-Islamic customs. In 1876 the Russian Empire annexed the region, bringing Russian settlers and Orthodox Christianity. The Soviet period pursued atheism, and after independence in 1991 the number of mosques grew from several dozen to several thousand, and Islam revived rapidly.

language.official: The official languages are Kyrgyz (the state language) and Russian.

ranking.name: Kyrgyz
ranking.description: Kyrgyz is the mother tongue of the Kyrgyz people, and the epic Manas is transmitted in it. It was made the state language in 1989; after independence the Kyrgyz share of the population rose to over 70 percent, villages and the south live almost entirely in Kyrgyz, and the government also requires civil servants to know the state language.

ranking.name: Uzbek
ranking.description: The Uzbeks have long lived in the agricultural towns of the Fergana Valley, and when the Soviet Union drew the boundaries of the union republics in 1924, Uzbek-populated areas such as Osh and Jalal-Abad were placed in Kyrgyzstan, so the south has many Uzbek speakers. In 1990 and 2010 bloody clashes between Kyrgyz and Uzbeks occurred in Osh.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Russian became the language of administration and education during the Russian imperial and Soviet periods, and after independence it remains an official language recognized by the constitution. Although only about 10 percent have Russian as a mother tongue, cities such as Bishkek use Russian heavily in business, academia and the media, and many people also work in Russia, so proficiency in Russian is high.

language.history: Kyrgyz belongs to the Turkic family; the Kyrgyz settled in the Tian Shan region around the 16th century and traditionally relied mainly on oral literature, with the epic Manas, hundreds of thousands of lines long, as a symbol of their national culture. From 1924 the Soviet Union created a written language for Kyrgyz, which switched to the Latin alphabet in 1928 and to Cyrillic in 1940. In the Soviet period Russian became the main language of education, administration and urban life. In 1989 Kyrgyz became the state language, and after independence Russian retains official status, the two languages being used side by side.

ranking.name: Beshbarmak
ranking.description: Boiled lamb or horse meat is chopped and mixed with wide noodle sheets, topped with meat broth and onions, and traditionally eaten by hand. The flavor rests mainly on salt and meat juices, emphasizing the natural taste of the meat.
ranking.history: Beshbarmak means "five fingers" in Turkic and is a guest-hosting dish shared by Kyrgyz and Kazakh nomads. At a traditional feast the host distributes different parts such as the sheep's head and leg according to the guests' age and status, reflecting the etiquette and seniority order of nomadic society. It is the main dish at weddings, funerals, memorial feasts and major festivals.

ranking.name: Central Asian plov
ranking.description: Rice, lamb, carrots and onions are braised in a large iron pot (kazan) and seasoned with cumin. The rice grains absorb lamb fat and meat juices and become glossy and richly flavored, and it is often eaten with tomato salad.
ranking.history: Plov is the representative dish of Central Asian settled agricultural culture, originating in ancient cities such as Bukhara and Samarkand; the Uzbek community of the Fergana Valley in southern Kyrgyzstan brought it in, and the plov of Osh is famous for using a local red rice variety. In the Soviet period, as people moved about, it became a festive dish throughout Central Asia, and today at weddings, circumcision feasts and funerals it is often cooked by men in big pots for hundreds of guests.

ranking.name: Lagman (hand-pulled noodles)
ranking.description: Long hand-pulled noodles topped with a thick sauce stir-fried from lamb, sweet peppers, tomatoes and vegetables. The noodles are thick and chewy, and the sauce is tangy, fragrant and slightly spicy; it is a common everyday noodle dish.
ranking.history: Lagman originates in the hand-pulled noodles of the Uyghurs and Hui (called Dungans in Central Asia) of Xinjiang, and its name probably comes from the Chinese "lamian" (pulled noodles). In the late 19th century, after the Qing dynasty put down the Hui rebellion in Shaanxi and Gansu, a group of Hui fled to Russian Central Asia (today's Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan), and Uyghurs also moved in one after another, bringing the technique of hand-pulled noodles. Today it has become an everyday noodle dish throughout Kyrgyzstan.

ranking.name: Manty (dumplings)
ranking.description: Large dumplings made by wrapping chopped lamb, onions and sheep fat in thin dough and steaming in multi-tiered steamers, often served with sour cream. Biting in releases the meat juices, and it is a common staple at family gatherings.
ranking.history: Manty is generally thought to be related to the filled-bun and mantou-type dough foods of the Mongol Empire, spreading across Central Asia, Turkey and the Caucasus with the Mongol westward campaigns of the 13th century, each region developing its own version. In Kyrgyzstan, steaming manty requires a special multi-tiered steamer (kaskan), and at family gatherings the women of the family often wrap them together.

ranking.name: Kymyz (fermented mare's milk)
ranking.description: A slightly sour drink made by churning and fermenting mare's milk in a leather bag or wooden barrel, containing a little alcohol. It tastes slightly sour with a little fizz, and is traditionally served and drunk in wooden bowls.
ranking.history: In summer the Kyrgyz drive their horse herds to high mountain pastures (jailoo) and milk the mares to make kymyz, a practice passed down on the Eurasian steppe for thousands of years. In summer kymyz is the nomads' main source of nutrition, and it is traditionally held in a leather bag (kökör). Today, at the turn of spring and summer, events are still held in many places to celebrate the first batch of kymyz, and in the epic Manas kymyz often symbolizes hospitality and abundance.
